## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

A 3-juan systematic mathematical classic in 100 problems-and-solutions, composed by Zhāng Qiūjiàn of Qīnghé in the late 5th or early 6th century. Structurally it follows the *Jiǔzhāng* problem-and-solution format but covers considerably more advanced material, with topics including:

- *Juàn shàng* (Upper): self-multiplication-and-division (*chéngchú*); right-triangle measurement (*gōugǔ cèwàng*) — problems 12-15 specifically on remote-sensing geometry; sum-and-difference relations of *gōugǔ*; redoubled-and-inverted *gōugǔ* configurations.
- *Juàn zhōng* (Middle): proportional distribution (*chāfēn*) and combined-with average-distribution (*jūnshū*); area-and-volume problems (*fāngyuán mìjī*); construction calculations (*shānggōng*); price-and-tax differences (*guìjiàn chāfēn*); arithmetic-progression problems; areal *fāngtián* fractional methods.
- *Juàn xià* (Lower): the famous *Hundred Fowls problem* (*bǎijī wèntí*); indeterminate-equation problems; deer-corral and granary three-volume problems with diagrams; *húshǐ* (arc-and-arrow) circular-segment problems.

The work's most famous contribution is the *Hundred Fowls problem*: a chicken costs 5 *qián*, a hen costs 3 *qián*, three chicks cost 1 *qián*; with 100 *qián* one purchases 100 fowls. How many of each? This is a system of two equations in three unknowns with positive-integer constraints — i.e., a problem in *indeterminate analysis*. The solution-procedure given is the foundation of pre-modern Chinese indeterminate-equation analysis and the historical predecessor of what would become the European *Diophantine analysis* tradition (Diophantus c. 250 CE worked on similar problems, but his work was lost to medieval Europe and only rediscovered in the Renaissance; the Chinese tradition's continuous engagement with such problems from Zhāng Qiūjiàn through Qín Jiǔsháo's 13th-century elaboration is independent of any Hellenistic transmission).

The Sìkù recension descends from Máo Jìn's 毛晉 (1599-1659) *Jígǔgé* 汲古閣 transcription of a Sòng manuscript fragment. The *Sòng* edition is the Northern Sòng imperial-secretariat collation by Zhào Yànruò 趙彦若, with the Zhēn Luán *shù yuē* 術曰 (procedure-says) annotations, the Liú Xiàosūn *cǎo yuē* 草曰 (procedure-elaboration-says) detailed working, and the Lǐ Chúnfēng *chén ... jǐn àn* 臣...謹按 imperial-annotated comments preserved together. The Sìkù editors collated the Máo Jìn transcription against the *Yǒnglè dàdiǎn* fragments and supplied missing diagrams (problems 12-15 of the *gōugǔ* section, the missing arc-and-arrow problem in the middle *juàn*, the deer-corral and three-volume problems in the lower *juàn*).

The *Sìkù* 提要 explicitly commends the work for its connection to ancient *Jiǔzhāng* methodology: "*[the work's] questions-and-answers cross-collate and clarify; in total 100 conditions, condensed-and-ancient in style, rather like the* Jiǔzhāng *and unlike the recent methods. But its threads-and-organization [are] refined-and-dense, truly able to deeply investigate the ancients' purport*". The Tang Imperial Academy thus made it a specialist text for advanced study.

For the broader *Suànjīng shíshū* context, see [KR3f0032](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0032), [KR3f0033](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0033), [KR3f0035](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0035), [KR3f0036](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0036), [KR3f0037](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0037), [KR3f0038](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0038). For the principal author, see [張邱建](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BC%B5%E9%82%B1%E5%BB%BA). For later Chinese indeterminate-analysis development, see Qín Jiǔsháo's *Shùshū jiǔzhāng* (=[KR3f0041](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR3/KR3f/KR3f0041) *Shùxué jiǔzhāng*).
